lines.name: POWER & ITS ABUSE
lines.question: Who holds authority, and what happens to the people who did not choose them.

subs.name: Abuse of Power
subs.definition: when someone with authority uses it to harm people or to serve themselves.

subs.name: Imperialism
subs.definition: when a stronger country takes control of another land and its people.

subs.name: Human Rights Violations
subs.definition: when people are denied the basic rights every person should have, like life, freedom and safety.

subs.name: Inequality
subs.definition: when some groups get fewer rights, chances or resources than others.

lines.name: CONFLICT
lines.question: Why people fight, and what is still unsettled when the fighting stops.

subs.name: Conflict
subs.definition: a struggle between groups, nations or ideas, from argument to war.

lines.name: IDENTITY & NATIONALISM
lines.question: Who a people say they are, and who that leaves out.

subs.name: Nationalism
subs.definition: a people's loyalty to their own nation, and the push for that nation to rule itself.

subs.name: Cultural Exchange and Diffusion
subs.definition: when ideas, beliefs, goods and ways of life spread from one people to another.

lines.name: WEALTH & RESOURCES
lines.question: Who owns what a place produces, and who does the producing.

subs.name: Economic Development
subs.definition: how a place grows its wealth, and who that growth helps or leaves behind.

subs.name: Scarcity
subs.definition: not having enough of something people need, like food, water or land.

lines.name: TECHNOLOGY & ENVIRONMENT
lines.question: What new tools let people do, and what they cost the world around them.

subs.name: Scientific and Technological Change
subs.definition: new knowledge and tools that change how people live and work.

subs.name: Environmental Crisis
subs.definition: serious harm to land, air, water or climate, often caused by people.

lines.name: A CONNECTED WORLD
lines.question: What happens when distant places start depending on each other.

subs.name: Cooperation
subs.definition: when groups or countries work together toward a shared goal.

subs.name: Population and Migration
subs.definition: how the number of people in a place changes, and why people move.

stops.title: Aurangzeb ends Mughal tolerance
stops.what_happened: The Mughal emperor Aurangzeb, a devout Muslim, brings back a tax on non-Muslims and dismisses his Hindu clerks. Hindu Indians remember his rule as oppressive for generations.

document.title: Aurangzeb and religious toleration
document.citation: Source: Donald J. Johnson et al., Through Indian Eyes, Apex Press, 1999 (adapted), from the NYS Global History and Geography II Regents Exam, June 2026

on_lines.reason: He uses the emperor's power to tax and push out the Hindus he rules, people who did not share his faith.
on_lines.question: Who holds authority, and what happens to the people who did not choose them.

exemplar.context: In the late 1600s, the Mughal Empire ruled most of India. Its emperors were Muslim, but most of the people they ruled were Hindu, and earlier emperors had practiced religious toleration.
exemplar.claim: Aurangzeb's rule shows the enduring issue of Abuse of Power, because he used the emperor's power against the Hindus he ruled.
exemplar.evidence: Document 2 shows that Aurangzeb “dismissed the Hindu clerks in his service” and brought back a tax on all “unbelievers.”
exemplar.explain: Hindus lost their jobs and paid an extra tax only because of their religion, and they had no say in it. That is abuse of power, and the document says Hindus remembered his “oppressive rule” for generations.

links.why: A generation earlier, Japan's shogun also punishes people for their faith.
links.explain: Both Aurangzeb and the Tokugawa shogun used their power against people of a different faith. However, Aurangzeb taxed Hindus and dismissed them from his service, while Japan's shogun paid informers to turn in Christians and their priests.

stops.title: The Ottomans fail at Vienna, and start to slip
stops.what_happened: The Ottoman army's last attempt to take Vienna fails. With no new conquests, and trade moving to the Americas and new sea routes, the empire begins a slow decline.

document.title: The decline of the Ottoman Empire
document.citation: Source: “Ottoman Empire (1301–1922),” BBC online, 2009 (adapted), from the NYS Global History and Geography Regents Exam, June 2015

on_lines.reason: Trade moves to the Americas and new routes, cheap goods from India and the Far East undercut Ottoman trade, and unemployment rises.
on_lines.question: Who owns what a place produces, and who does the producing.

on_lines.reason: The document starts the decline with a lost war: the failed attempt to conquer Vienna in 1683.
on_lines.question: Why people fight, and what is still unsettled when the fighting stops.

exemplar.context: In the late 1600s, the Ottoman Empire was still huge, built on conquest and on the trade routes between Europe and Asia. That trade was starting to move elsewhere.
exemplar.claim: The Ottoman decline shows the enduring issue of Economic Development, because the empire's wealth depended on trade it was losing.
exemplar.evidence: Document 3 shows the causes: “competition from trade from the Americas,” “cheap products from India and the Far East” and the “development of other trade routes,” along with “rising unemployment within the Empire.”
exemplar.explain: When trade moved to new routes, money and jobs left the empire with it. A country's wealth depends on what it produces and trades, and when that changes, the whole empire feels it.

u4.context: In the late 1600s, the Ottoman Empire was still huge, built on conquest and on the trade routes between Europe and Asia. That trade was starting to move elsewhere.
u4.claim: The Ottoman decline shows the enduring issue of Economic Development, because the empire's wealth depended on trade it was losing.
u4.evidence: Document 3 shows the causes: “competition from trade from the Americas,” “cheap products from India and the Far East” and the “development of other trade routes,” along with “rising unemployment within the Empire.”
u4.explain: When trade moved to new routes, money and jobs left the empire with it. A country's wealth depends on what it produces and trades, and when that changes, the whole empire feels it.

u2.context: In 1683, the Ottoman Empire had been growing by war for more than two hundred years, taking land in the Balkans, the Middle East and North Africa. Vienna, the Hapsburg capital, was its next target.
u2.claim: The siege of Vienna shows the enduring issue of Conflict, because a lost war ended the Ottomans' growth.
u2.evidence: Document 3 shows that the “last attempt was made to conquer Vienna” in 1683 and “it failed,” and that without new conquests the empire “lost momentum and went into a slow decline.”
u2.explain: The empire was built by conquest, so when the fighting stopped going its way, so did its growth. Conflict decides who holds land, and after 1683 the Ottomans stopped gaining it.

links.why: Two centuries later, the empire that failed at Vienna is losing its hold on the Balkans.
links.explain: The Ottoman Empire's decline contributed to the Balkan crisis because a weaker empire could no longer hold its Balkan lands. By 1912 the small Balkan nations were ready to drive it out of Europe, and the great powers rushed to protect their own interests.

stops.title: Jahangir opens his ports to the English
stops.what_happened: The Mughal emperor Jahangir answers a letter from King James I of England. He orders every port in his empire to welcome English merchants and let them live, buy and sell freely.

document.title: Emperor Jahangir’s letter to King James I of England, 1617
document.citation: Source: Modified version of the Letter to James I, King of England, 1617, published on the Fordham University Indian History Sourcebook

on_lines.reason: Two rulers trade gifts and promises, and Jahangir orders his whole empire to welcome English merchants as "the subjects of my friend."
on_lines.question: What happens when distant places start depending on each other.

on_lines.reason: English merchants may now live anywhere in the empire, and buy, sell and carry goods home to England.
on_lines.question: Who a people say they are, and who that leaves out.

exemplar.context: In 1617, English merchants wanted to trade in India, which was ruled by the powerful Mughal Empire. King James I of England sent an ambassador, Sir Thomas Roe, with gifts and a letter.
exemplar.claim: Jahangir's letter shows the enduring issue of Cooperation, because two rulers far apart agree to work together for trade.
exemplar.evidence: Document 5 shows Jahangir ordering “all the kingdoms and ports” of his empire to receive English merchants “as the subjects of my friend,” free “to sell, buy, and to transport into their country.”
exemplar.explain: Two rulers who never met trade gifts and promises, and both of their countries gain from the trade that follows. Cooperation is working together toward a shared goal, and this letter opens the door for England in India.

u6.context: In 1617, English merchants wanted to trade in India, which was ruled by the powerful Mughal Empire. King James I of England sent an ambassador, Sir Thomas Roe, with gifts and a letter.
u6.claim: Jahangir's letter shows the enduring issue of Cooperation, because two rulers far apart agree to work together for trade.
u6.evidence: Document 5 shows Jahangir ordering “all the kingdoms and ports” of his empire to receive English merchants “as the subjects of my friend,” free “to sell, buy, and to transport into their country.”
u6.explain: Two rulers who never met trade gifts and promises, and both of their countries gain from the trade that follows. Cooperation is working together toward a shared goal, and this letter opens the door for England in India.

u3.context: In 1617, the Mughal emperor Jahangir answered a letter from King James I of England. English merchants wanted to live and do business in India.
u3.claim: Jahangir's letter shows the enduring issue of Cultural Exchange and Diffusion, because it opens India to English people and English trade.
u3.evidence: Document 5 shows Jahangir promising that “in what place soever they choose to live, they may have free liberty without any restraint,” and that they may “sell, buy, and to transport into their country” what they want.
u3.explain: When foreign merchants can live, buy and sell anywhere in an empire, goods and ideas move both ways between the two peoples. That exchange between India and England starts with an open door like this one.

links.why: Eighteen years later, Japan answers the same question the opposite way.
links.explain: Both Jahangir and the Tokugawa shogun had to decide what to do about European traders arriving in Asia. However, Jahangir opened every port in his empire to English merchants, while Japan's shogun closed the country and forbade any Japanese to leave.

stops.title: Japan closes its doors
stops.what_happened: The Tokugawa government forbids any Japanese person to leave the country, on pain of death. It also pays rewards to anyone who turns in a Christian.

document.title: Edict of 1635 Ordering the Closing of Japan
document.citation: Source: David John Lu, Sources of Japanese History, McGraw-Hill, from the NYS Global History and Geography Regents Exam, January 2005

on_lines.reason: Japan cuts off the flow of people and ideas: no one may leave, anyone who returns dies, and Christian teaching is hunted down.
on_lines.question: Who a people say they are, and who that leaves out.

on_lines.reason: People are put to death for traveling abroad, and informers are paid to reveal where Christians are.
on_lines.question: Who holds authority, and what happens to the people who did not choose them.

exemplar.context: In the early 1600s, European traders and Catholic missionaries, called padres, were arriving in Japan, and some Japanese had become Christians. The Tokugawa shoguns saw them as a threat to their control.
exemplar.claim: The Edict of 1635 shows the enduring issue of Cultural Exchange and Diffusion, because Japan's government shut down the flow of people and ideas in and out of the country.
exemplar.evidence: Document 4 shows that “no Japanese is permitted to go abroad,” and that anyone who returns from overseas “must be put to death.” It also pays informers who reveal “the followers of padres (Christians).”
exemplar.explain: Cultural exchange needs people to travel and ideas to spread, and this law stops both. Japan chose to close itself off, the opposite of trading and sharing with the world.

u3.context: In the early 1600s, European traders and Catholic missionaries, called padres, were arriving in Japan, and some Japanese had become Christians. The Tokugawa shoguns saw them as a threat to their control.
u3.claim: The Edict of 1635 shows the enduring issue of Cultural Exchange and Diffusion, because Japan's government shut down the flow of people and ideas in and out of the country.
u3.evidence: Document 4 shows that “no Japanese is permitted to go abroad,” and that anyone who returns from overseas “must be put to death.” It also pays informers who reveal “the followers of padres (Christians).”
u3.explain: Cultural exchange needs people to travel and ideas to spread, and this law stops both. Japan chose to close itself off, the opposite of trading and sharing with the world.

u1.context: In 1635, the Tokugawa shoguns had ruled Japan for about thirty years and wanted no outside threats. They feared Christianity and contact with foreigners.
u1.claim: The Edict of 1635 shows the enduring issue of Human Rights Violations, because people could be killed for traveling or for their faith.
u1.evidence: Document 4 shows that anyone who tries to leave Japan secretly “must be executed,” and that an informer who reveals where a high-ranking padre is gets “one hundred pieces of silver.”
u1.explain: The freedom to travel and to practice your faith are basic rights every person should have, and this law punishes both with death. The shogun's government treats its own people as threats to be hunted.

links.why: Eighteen years earlier, the Mughal emperor opened his ports instead.
links.explain: Both the Tokugawa shogun and Jahangir were powerful Asian rulers deciding how to deal with Europeans. However, Japan closed itself off to protect the shogun's control, while Jahangir welcomed English merchants as the subjects of his friend.

stops.title: The Tōkaidō: the shogun's road
stops.what_happened: The Tokugawa shoguns run Japan's most important highway as a government road. Their messengers go first, and checkpoints keep ordinary travelers off it at night.

document.title: The Tōkaidō — the road that governed Japan
document.citation: Source: Patricia J. Graham, “The Political and Economic Importance of the Tōkaidō,” Tōkaidō: Adventures on the Road in Old Japan, University of Kansas Spencer Museum of Art (adapted), from the NYS Global History and Geography Regents Exam, January 2012

on_lines.reason: The shogun decides who may travel and when, and barriers and checkpoints let the government control movement across Japan.
on_lines.question: Who holds authority, and what happens to the people who did not choose them.

exemplar.context: In the 1600s, the Tokugawa shoguns ruled Japan after a long civil war between powerful lords. Keeping control of distant provinces was their biggest challenge.
exemplar.claim: The Tōkaidō shows the enduring issue of Abuse of Power, because the shogun used the road to control where and when ordinary people could move.
exemplar.evidence: Document 6 shows that government messengers “could freely pass government road barriers at all times of the day or night,” but “private citizens were not allowed to travel at night,” and “barriers and checkpoints” kept them off the road.
exemplar.explain: The road is open for the government and closed to everyone else. Watching and limiting how ordinary people move is one way a ruler uses authority to serve himself.

links.why: Louis XIV controls his nobles the other way: he makes them stay.
links.explain: Both the Tokugawa shoguns and Louis XIV kept power by controlling the people who could challenge them. However, the shogun controlled who could travel on Japan's roads, while Louis XIV made his nobles stay at Versailles, where he could watch them.

stops._note: Packet Day 4 anchor: Power & Its Abuse.

stops.title: Louis XIV keeps his nobles at Versailles
stops.what_happened: Louis XIV moves the French court out of Paris to his palace at Versailles. He expects the nobles to stay there under his eye, and to spend until they depend on him.

document.title: The court at Versailles
document.citation: Source: The Memoirs of the Duke de Saint-Simon, ed. F. Arkwright, Brentano's, Vol. V (adapted), via the Internet Modern History Sourcebook, Fordham University

on_lines.reason: Louis watches every noble at court and makes them live beyond their income until they depend on him, so no one can rival his power.
on_lines.question: Who holds authority, and what happens to the people who did not choose them.

exemplar.context: In 1682, Louis XIV, who ruled France as an absolute monarch, moved his court to Versailles. As a boy he had lived through the Fronde, a revolt by French nobles, and he never trusted them again.
exemplar.claim: Versailles shows the enduring issue of Abuse of Power, because Louis XIV used his court to control the nobles and make them depend on him.
exemplar.evidence: Document 7 shows Saint-Simon writing that Louis “saw everybody,” and that by making expensive habits a necessity, “he compelled his courtiers to live beyond their income.”
exemplar.explain: Nobles who are watched all day and owe the king money can't plot against him. Louis keeps all the power in his own hands by making the most powerful people in France helpless.

links.why: About a century later, Sieyès says the people who paid for all of it have counted for nothing.
links.explain: The spending of France's kings contributed to the anger of the Third Estate because the splendor of Versailles and the kings' wars were paid for with taxes that fell on the common people. By 1789 France was deep in debt, and Sieyès said the people who paid for everything had counted for nothing.

stops._note: Packet Day 4 anchor: Power & Its Abuse. 1682 is the year the court moved to Versailles.

stops.title: Locke: the people can take power back
stops.what_happened: John Locke argues that people form governments to protect their life, liberty and property. A government that grabs absolute power breaks the deal, and the people may take their power back.

document.title: Locke on why people leave the state of nature
document.citation: Source: John Locke, Two Treatises of Government, 1690

also_read.title: Locke on a government that breaks the deal
also_read.citation: Source: John Locke, Two Treatises on Civil Government

on_lines.reason: Locke names the danger: a government that takes "absolute power" over people's lives and liberties loses its right to rule.
on_lines.question: Who holds authority, and what happens to the people who did not choose them.

exemplar.context: In 1688, England's Parliament pushed out King James II in the Glorious Revolution. John Locke wrote to explain when people have the right to replace their government.
exemplar.claim: Locke's writing shows the enduring issue of Abuse of Power, because he says a government that takes absolute power loses its right to rule.
exemplar.evidence: Document 2 shows Locke writing that when lawmakers grab “an absolute power over their lives, liberties, and estates of the people,” they “forfeit the power,” and it passes to the people, “who have a right to resume their original liberty.”
exemplar.explain: People form governments to protect their life, liberty and property, not to lose them. Locke sets a limit on power: a government that abuses it breaks the deal, and the people can take their power back.

links.why: A century later, France writes Locke's rights into law, with resistance to oppression among them.
links.explain: Locke's ideas contributed to the Declaration of the Rights of Man because they gave French revolutionaries a reason to resist a government that abused its power. The Declaration names the natural rights Locke described, liberty and property, and adds resistance to oppression.

stops.title: Montesquieu: divide the power
stops.what_happened: Montesquieu argues that if the same person or group makes the laws, enforces them and judges them, there is no liberty. Power has to be divided.

document.title: Montesquieu on the power of judging
document.citation: Source: Montesquieu, The Spirit of the Laws

also_read.title: Montesquieu on powers united in one person
also_read.citation: Source: Baron de Montesquieu, Spirit of the Laws

on_lines.reason: He warns that when lawmaking and enforcing sit in one set of hands, "tyrannical laws" follow.
on_lines.question: Who holds authority, and what happens to the people who did not choose them.

exemplar.context: In the 1700s, French kings made the laws, enforced them, and had the final word in the courts. Montesquieu studied governments around the world to find out what keeps people free.
exemplar.claim: Montesquieu's writing shows the enduring issue of Abuse of Power, because he warns what happens when one person holds all the power.
exemplar.evidence: Document 4 shows Montesquieu writing that when the lawmaking and enforcing powers “are united in the same person,” there “can be no liberty,” because that ruler might “enact tyrannical laws to execute them in a tyrannical manner.”
exemplar.explain: If one ruler makes the laws and enforces them, nothing stops him from using them against the people. Dividing power is Montesquieu's way to stop abuse of power before it starts.

links.why: In 1793 the Law of Suspects makes the courts the enforcement arm of the government, the danger Montesquieu named.
links.explain: Both Montesquieu and the Law of Suspects deal with who controls the courts. However, Montesquieu warned that judges must be separate from the lawmakers and the government, while the Law of Suspects made the courts the enforcement arm of the government, the danger he described.

stops.title: Rousseau: the general will
stops.what_happened: Jean-Jacques Rousseau asks how people can live under a government and still stay free. His answer is the social contract: the people unite, and the law follows the general will, the common good.

document.title: Rousseau states the problem the social contract solves
document.citation: Source: Jean-Jacques Rousseau, The Social Contract, 1762. Translated by G. D. H. Cole, 1913. Book I, Chapter VI.

also_read.title: Rousseau distinguishes the general will from the will of all
also_read.citation: Source: Jean-Jacques Rousseau, The Social Contract, 1762. Translated by G. D. H. Cole, 1913. Book II, Chapter III.

on_lines.reason: Rousseau says a people united can govern itself and each person can still "obey himself alone." A people ruling itself is the idea nationalists build on.
on_lines.question: Who a people say they are, and who that leaves out.

on_lines.reason: The casefile asks the hard question: what happens when a leader claims to speak for the general will and jails the people who disagree?
on_lines.question: Who holds authority, and what happens to the people who did not choose them.

exemplar.context: In the 1700s, most Europeans lived under kings who said their power came from God. Rousseau asked how people could live under a government and still be free.
exemplar.claim: Rousseau's Social Contract shows the enduring issue of Nationalism, because it says a people united together should rule themselves.
exemplar.evidence: Document 5 shows Rousseau looking for a way of living together in which each person, “while uniting himself with all, may still obey himself alone, and remain as free as before.”
exemplar.explain: If the people united are the ones who rule, then power belongs to the people, not to a king. Nationalists build on that idea: a people who share one identity should govern themselves.

u3.context: In the 1700s, most Europeans lived under kings who said their power came from God. Rousseau asked how people could live under a government and still be free.
u3.claim: Rousseau's Social Contract shows the enduring issue of Nationalism, because it says a people united together should rule themselves.
u3.evidence: Document 5 shows Rousseau looking for a way of living together in which each person, “while uniting himself with all, may still obey himself alone, and remain as free as before.”
u3.explain: If the people united are the ones who rule, then power belongs to the people, not to a king. Nationalists build on that idea: a people who share one identity should govern themselves.

u1.context: In 1762, Rousseau wrote that law should follow the general will, the common good of the whole people. Later leaders would claim that they knew what the general will was.
u1.claim: Rousseau's idea of the general will connects to the enduring issue of Abuse of Power, because a leader can claim to speak for everyone and punish those who disagree.
u1.evidence: Document 6 shows Rousseau saying the general will “takes account only of the common interest,” while the will of all is “no more than a sum of particular wills.”
u1.explain: If the general will can be different from what people actually want, someone has to decide what it is. A leader who says he alone knows the common good can use that claim to silence anyone who disagrees.

links.why: Robespierre claims to speak for the homeland, and the Law of Suspects removes anyone who might sabotage the general will.
links.explain: Rousseau's idea of the general will contributed to the Reign of Terror because it gave revolutionary leaders a way to claim they spoke for the whole people. Robespierre's government used that claim to remove anyone who might sabotage the general will.

links.why: France's Declaration calls law “the expression of the general will.”
links.explain: Rousseau's idea of the general will contributed to the Declaration of the Rights of Man because it said the people, not a king, should be the source of law. Article 6 of the Declaration put that idea into French law: “Law is the expression of the general will.”

stops.title: Catherine the Great: equal laws, except for serfs
stops.what_happened: Catherine the Great writes that all citizens should be subject to the same laws. The same year, her government orders serfs to obey their landlords absolutely, and punishes any who complain to her.

document.title: Catherine the Great on law and equality
document.citation: Source: Documents of Catherine the Great, W. F. Reddaway, ed., Cambridge University Press (adapted)

also_read.title: Catherine's government on serfs
also_read.citation: Source: A Source Book for Russian History, G. Vernadsky, trans., Yale University Press, 1972 (adapted)

on_lines.reason: Her own words say everyone answers to the same laws, but serfs owe their landlords "absolute obedience" and may not even complain.
on_lines.question: Who holds authority, and what happens to the people who did not choose them.

on_lines.reason: Serfs who petition the empress are whipped with the knout and sent to forced labor for life.
on_lines.question: Who holds authority, and what happens to the people who did not choose them.

exemplar.context: In 1767, Catherine the Great ruled Russia and wrote to the Enlightenment thinkers of her day. Most Russians were serfs, peasants bound to their landlords' land.
exemplar.claim: Catherine's Russia shows the enduring issue of Inequality, because her government promised equal laws but kept serfs under their landlords' control.
exemplar.evidence: Document 9 shows Catherine writing that “the Equality of the Citizens consists in this; that they should all be subject to the same Laws.” Yet Document 10 shows her Senate ordering that serfs owe their landlords “proper submission and absolute obedience in all matters.”
exemplar.explain: Equal laws for citizens meant nothing to serfs, who had to obey their landlords in everything. The gap between her words and her laws is inequality: some people get rights, and others don't.

u1-inequality.context: In 1767, Catherine the Great ruled Russia and wrote to the Enlightenment thinkers of her day. Most Russians were serfs, peasants bound to their landlords' land.
u1-inequality.claim: Catherine's Russia shows the enduring issue of Inequality, because her government promised equal laws but kept serfs under their landlords' control.
u1-inequality.evidence: Document 9 shows Catherine writing that “the Equality of the Citizens consists in this; that they should all be subject to the same Laws.” Yet Document 10 shows her Senate ordering that serfs owe their landlords “proper submission and absolute obedience in all matters.”
u1-inequality.explain: Equal laws for citizens meant nothing to serfs, who had to obey their landlords in everything. The gap between her words and her laws is inequality: some people get rights, and others don't.

u1-abuse-of-power.context: In 1767, Russian serfs could not leave their landlords' land, and many were treated harshly. Some tried to petition the empress herself for help.
u1-abuse-of-power.claim: Catherine's decree on serfs shows the enduring issue of Abuse of Power, because the government punished people just for asking for help.
u1-abuse-of-power.evidence: Document 10 shows that serfs who complained about their landlords, “and especially to petition Her Imperial Majesty personally,” would be “punished by the knout” and sent to “penal servitude” for life.
u1-abuse-of-power.explain: Asking the ruler for help should be a right, but here it earns a whipping and forced labor for life. A government that punishes complaints uses its power to protect the powerful, not the people.

links.why: In France, the people who carry the country on their backs say they have counted for nothing.
links.explain: Both Catherine's Russia and France before 1789 were built on the work of peasants who had little power. However, Russia's serfs could be whipped and sent to forced labor just for complaining, while in France the Third Estate was about to demand a voice.

stops.title: Two voices against the slave trade
stops.what_happened: In 1789, William Wilberforce tells Parliament the slave trade must be abolished. Olaudah Equiano tells his own story of being carried below decks across the Atlantic to work for strangers.

document.title: Two voices from 1789: the slave trade
document.citation: Source: William Wilberforce, speech to the House of Commons, May 1789, in Cobbett, Parliamentary History of England, vol. 28 (adapted)

also_read.title: Olaudah Equiano's narrative
also_read.citation: Source: Olaudah Equiano, The Interesting Narrative of the Life of Olaudah Equiano, London, 1794 edition (adapted), via OER Project

on_lines.reason: Equiano is taken from his country with no chance of return and packed below decks; Wilberforce calls the trade a wickedness that must end.
on_lines.question: Who holds authority, and what happens to the people who did not choose them.

on_lines.reason: Equiano is moved across an ocean by force, never to return home: a migration no one chose.
on_lines.question: What happens when distant places start depending on each other.

exemplar.context: In 1789, millions of Africans had already been carried across the Atlantic to work as slaves in the Americas. In Britain, people were starting to argue that the trade should end.
exemplar.claim: The Atlantic slave trade shows the enduring issue of Human Rights Violations, because people were taken from their homes and forced to work for strangers.
exemplar.evidence: Document 8 shows Equiano writing that he was robbed “of all chance of returning to my native country” and was told “we were to be carried to these white people's country to work for them.”
exemplar.explain: Being taken from your home, packed below decks and forced to work without pay takes away a person's freedom and dignity. Even Wilberforce, speaking in Parliament, calls the trade a “wickedness” that must be abolished.

u1.context: In 1789, millions of Africans had already been carried across the Atlantic to work as slaves in the Americas. In Britain, people were starting to argue that the trade should end.
u1.claim: The Atlantic slave trade shows the enduring issue of Human Rights Violations, because people were taken from their homes and forced to work for strangers.
u1.evidence: Document 8 shows Equiano writing that he was robbed “of all chance of returning to my native country” and was told “we were to be carried to these white people's country to work for them.”
u1.explain: Being taken from your home, packed below decks and forced to work without pay takes away a person's freedom and dignity. Even Wilberforce, speaking in Parliament, calls the trade a “wickedness” that must be abolished.

u6.context: In the 1700s, the Atlantic slave trade was moving millions of Africans to the Americas. It was one of the largest forced migrations in history.
u6.claim: Equiano's story shows the enduring issue of Population and Migration, because he was moved across an ocean by force, with no way home.
u6.evidence: Document 8 shows Equiano being “put down under the decks” and learning that “we were to be carried to these white people's country to work for them.”
u6.explain: Most migrants choose to move, but Equiano had no choice and no chance of return. Forced migration on this scale moved whole populations and changed who lives in the Americas to this day.

links.why: Two years later, enslaved people in Saint-Domingue take their freedom by force.
links.explain: Before 1791, people like Equiano and Wilberforce spoke out against slavery, but enslaved people had not won their freedom anywhere in the Caribbean. In 1791, enslaved people in Saint-Domingue rose up and began to take their freedom by force. After that, Haiti became the first nation to end slavery by revolution, and slaveholders everywhere feared it would happen again.

stops._note: Document 8 prints two sources: Wilberforce (lead) and Equiano (also_read).

stops.title: Wollstonecraft: what about women?
stops.what_happened: Mary Wollstonecraft writes to a member of France's National Assembly. If women are shut out of the new constitution, she says, the men who wrote it are acting like tyrants.

document.title: Wollstonecraft on reason and the rights of women
document.citation: Source: Mary Wollstonecraft, A Vindication of the Rights of Woman, 1792. Addressed to Talleyrand-Périgord, a member of the French National Assembly.

on_lines.reason: Women are left out of the new rights, and she says only one thing could justify it: proof that women lack reason.
on_lines.question: Who holds authority, and what happens to the people who did not choose them.

exemplar.context: In 1791, France wrote a new constitution after its Revolution, but women could not vote or hold office under it. Mary Wollstonecraft, an English writer, answered by writing to one of the men who made it.
exemplar.claim: Wollstonecraft's writing shows the enduring issue of Inequality, because women were left out of the rights the Revolution promised.
exemplar.evidence: Document 7 shows Wollstonecraft writing that if women are “to be excluded,” the men in charge must “prove first” that women lack reason, or else the “flaw in your NEW CONSTITUTION” will show they “act like a tyrant.”
exemplar.explain: The Revolution promised rights to all, but it gave them only to men. Wollstonecraft shows that leaving half the people out for no good reason is inequality, the same unfairness the Revolution said it was ending.

links.why: A year earlier in Paris, Olympe de Gouges rewrote France's declaration for women.
links.explain: Both Wollstonecraft and Olympe de Gouges argued that the Revolution's rights must include women. However, Wollstonecraft wrote from England about women's reason and education, while Olympe de Gouges, in Paris, rewrote the Declaration itself article by article.

stops.title: The Third Estate: everything, and nothing
stops.what_happened: On the eve of the Revolution, Abbé Sieyès says the Third Estate, the common people, is everything in France and has counted for nothing. A popular cartoon shows a peasant carrying a priest and a noble on his back.

document.title: Abbé Sieyès asks what the Third Estate actually is
document.citation: Source: Abbé Sieyès, 1789 (adapted), from the New Visions Global History II Exam Question Bank, Part 1, citing the NYS Global History and Geography Regents Exam, August 2014

also_read.title: “Le Grand Abus” (“The Great Abuse”)
also_read.citation: Source: The Way We Saw It: ..., Highsmith, Inc., 1998 (adapted), from the New Visions Global History II Exam Question Bank, Part 1, citing the NYS Global History and Geography Regents Exam, August 2002

on_lines.reason: Sieyès's three answers, everything, nothing, something, and the cartoon's bent-over peasant show who carries France and who rides.
on_lines.question: Who holds authority, and what happens to the people who did not choose them.

exemplar.context: In 1789, French society was still split into three estates: the clergy, the nobles, and everyone else. The Third Estate was almost all of the people, and it paid most of the taxes.
exemplar.claim: The Third Estate shows the enduring issue of Inequality, because the people who did the work and paid the taxes had no power.
exemplar.evidence: Document 1 shows Sieyès saying the Third Estate is “Everything” but has been “Nothing” in the political order, and Document 2 shows a bent-over peasant carrying a priest and a noble on his back.
exemplar.explain: The Third Estate carries France the way the peasant carries the priest and the noble. When most people pay for everything and have no voice, that is inequality, and it is what the Revolution set out to end.

links.why: The same year, the National Assembly declares that men are born free and equal in rights.
links.explain: Before 1789, the Third Estate had been nothing in the political order, and birth decided a person's rights. In 1789, the National Assembly declared that men are born and remain free and equal in rights. After that, the old privileges of the clergy and nobles could no longer be defended by law.

stops.title: The Declaration of the Rights of Man
stops.what_happened: France's new National Assembly declares that men are born and remain free and equal in rights. Law is to be the expression of the general will, and every citizen has a right to take part in making it.

document.title: Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen, 1789
document.citation: Source: The Avalon Project at Yale Law School (adapted), from the New Visions Global History II Exam Question Bank, Part 1, citing the NYS Global History and Geography II Regents Exam, June 2019

on_lines.reason: It says men are "born and remain free and equal in rights," ending the old rule that birth decides your rights. Document 4 asks who it still left out.
on_lines.question: Who holds authority, and what happens to the people who did not choose them.

exemplar.context: In 1789, the Third Estate broke away and named itself the National Assembly. That summer it wrote down the rights it said every French citizen should have.
exemplar.claim: The Declaration of the Rights of Man shows the enduring issue of Inequality, because it tries to end a system where birth decided your rights.
exemplar.evidence: Document 3 shows Article 1 saying “men are born and remain free and equal in rights,” and Article 6 saying all citizens are “equally eligible to all dignities and to all public positions” by their abilities.
exemplar.explain: Under the old system, nobles got the top jobs because of who their parents were. The Declaration says ability, not birth, should decide, though it says “men,” and women would soon ask whether it meant them too.

links.why: Two years later, Olympe de Gouges rewrites it for women.
links.explain: The Declaration of the Rights of Man contributed to Olympe de Gouges's declaration because it promised equal rights but spoke only of men. She copied its articles and added woman, to show exactly who it had left out.

links.why: In Saint-Domingue, Toussaint L'Ouverture fights for the same Liberty and Equality.
links.explain: The Declaration of the Rights of Man contributed to the Haitian Revolution because its ideas of liberty and equality reached France's colony of Saint-Domingue. Toussaint L'Ouverture used those same words to call enslaved people to fight for their freedom.

stops.title: Olympe de Gouges: the rights of woman
stops.what_happened: Olympe de Gouges rewrites the Declaration for women. Woman is born free and equal to man in rights, she writes, and the only limit on those rights has been the tyranny of men.

document.title: Olympe de Gouges, Declaration of the Rights of Woman and of the Female Citizen, 1791
document.citation: Source: Olympe de Gouges, 1791 (adapted), from the New Visions Global History II Exam Question Bank, Part 1, citing the NYS Global History and Geography II Regents Exam, June 2019

on_lines.reason: She keeps the Declaration's own words and adds woman to them, showing exactly who the first version left out.
on_lines.question: Who holds authority, and what happens to the people who did not choose them.

exemplar.context: In 1791, women still could not vote or hold office in France, even after the National Assembly declared the Rights of Man. Olympe de Gouges, a writer in Paris, answered.
exemplar.claim: Olympe de Gouges's declaration shows the enduring issue of Inequality, because it shows exactly who the Rights of Man left out.
exemplar.evidence: Document 4 shows her first article saying “woman is born free and remains equal to man in rights,” and her claim that the only limit on women's rights has been “the perpetual tyranny of man.”
exemplar.explain: She copies the Declaration's own words and adds woman, so the gap is impossible to miss. A promise of equal rights that leaves out half the people is still inequality.

links.why: A year later in London, Mary Wollstonecraft makes the same argument.
links.explain: Both Olympe de Gouges and Mary Wollstonecraft said women were being left out of the rights the Revolution promised. However, Olympe de Gouges answered by rewriting France's own Declaration for women, while Wollstonecraft argued that only proof that women lack reason could justify shutting them out.

stops.title: The Reign of Terror
stops.what_happened: With France at war and divided, Robespierre and the National Convention pass the Law of Suspects. Revolutionary courts send thousands to their deaths, and most of them are peasants and workers, not nobles.

document.title: Maximilien Robespierre, “In Defence of the Committee of Public Safety and Against Briez,” September 25, 1793
document.citation: Source: Maximilien Robespierre, in Virtue and Terror, Verso (adapted), from the New Visions Global History II Exam Question Bank, Part 1, citing the NYS Global History and Geography Regents Exam, January 2015

also_read.title: About the Law of Suspects: a historians' summary
also_read.citation: Source: Liberty, Equality, Fraternity: Exploring the French Revolution (Roy Rosenzweig Center for History and New Media / American Social History Project) (adapted), from the New Visions Global History II Exam Question Bank, Part 1, citing the NYS Global History and Geography Regents Exam, January 2015

also_read.title: Executions During the Reign of Terror (chart)
also_read.citation: Source: Dennis Sherman et al., eds., World Civilizations: Sources, Images, and Interpretations, McGraw-Hill (adapted), from the New Visions Global History II Exam Question Bank, Part 1, citing the NYS Global History and Geography Regents Exam, August 2006

on_lines.reason: The Law of Suspects turns the courts into the government's weapon against anyone suspected of being an enemy of the Republic.
on_lines.question: Who holds authority, and what happens to the people who did not choose them.

on_lines.reason: People can be tried and put to death on suspicion, and the chart shows most of the executed were peasants and workers.
on_lines.question: Who holds authority, and what happens to the people who did not choose them.

on_lines.reason: Robespierre defends the Terror as a war: "a Republic surrounded by enemies," foreign and inside France.
on_lines.question: Why people fight, and what is still unsettled when the fighting stops.

exemplar.context: In 1793, France was at war with much of Europe and fighting rebels at home. Robespierre and the Committee of Public Safety took control of the government.
exemplar.claim: The Reign of Terror shows the enduring issue of Abuse of Power, because the government turned the courts into a weapon against its own people.
exemplar.evidence: Document 6 shows that the Law of Suspects created courts to try anyone “suspected of treason against the Republic,” and in effect “made the penal justice system into the enforcement arm of the revolutionary government.”
exemplar.explain: Courts are supposed to protect people from the government, but here they work for it. A government that can put people to death on suspicion has power with no limit.

u1-abuse-of-power.context: In 1793, France was at war with much of Europe and fighting rebels at home. Robespierre and the Committee of Public Safety took control of the government.
u1-abuse-of-power.claim: The Reign of Terror shows the enduring issue of Abuse of Power, because the government turned the courts into a weapon against its own people.
u1-abuse-of-power.evidence: Document 6 shows that the Law of Suspects created courts to try anyone “suspected of treason against the Republic,” and in effect “made the penal justice system into the enforcement arm of the revolutionary government.”
u1-abuse-of-power.explain: Courts are supposed to protect people from the government, but here they work for it. A government that can put people to death on suspicion has power with no limit.

u1-human-rights-violations.context: In 1793 and 1794, during the Reign of Terror, revolutionary courts sent thousands of people to the guillotine. The Revolution had begun by declaring the rights of man.
u1-human-rights-violations.claim: The Reign of Terror shows the enduring issue of Human Rights Violations, because people could be put to death on suspicion, and most of the dead were ordinary people.
u1-human-rights-violations.evidence: Document 7 shows that 3,961 peasants and 4,389 working-class people were executed, more than the nobles and clergy put together.
u1-human-rights-violations.explain: The Revolution promised liberty and security to every citizen, but thousands lost their lives on suspicion alone. When your right to life depends on whether the government trusts you, human rights are being violated.

u2.context: In 1793, France's revolutionary government was at war with Austria, Prussia and Britain, and fighting rebels inside France. Robespierre defended the harsh measures of the Committee of Public Safety.
u2.claim: The Terror shows the enduring issue of Conflict, because war inside and outside France was the reason given for it.
u2.evidence: Document 5 shows Robespierre warning of “the foreigners and internal enemies” and describing “a Republic surrounded by enemies.”
u2.explain: Robespierre uses the war to explain why the government needs so much power. Conflict made the Terror possible: when a country is fighting for its life, leaders can call anyone who disagrees an enemy.

links.why: The Republic's war at home becomes one general's war across Europe.
links.explain: Before Napoleon, revolutionary France was ruled by assemblies and committees, like the one that ran the Terror. In 1804, Napoleon, a general, crowned himself emperor. After that, France's wars were no longer about defending the Revolution but about building an empire across Europe.

stops._note: Documents 5–7 are one event. Lead document: Robespierre (5). Peasants 28 + working class 31 on the chart: 'most'.

stops.title: Napoleon's empire at its height
stops.what_happened: By 1812 Napoleon's France controls or dominates most of Europe. The map marks the battles that built it.

document.title: Napoleon's Empire, 1812 (map)
document.citation: Source: Peiser and Serber, Our World, AMSCO (adapted), from the New Visions Global History II Exam Question Bank, Part 1, citing the NYS Global History and Geography Regents Exam, January 2005

on_lines.reason: France rules some lands directly and others through rulers it controls; the map's key shows both.
on_lines.question: Who holds authority, and what happens to the people who did not choose them.

on_lines.reason: The battle sites across the map show the empire was built by war.
on_lines.question: Why people fight, and what is still unsettled when the fighting stops.

exemplar.context: In 1812, Napoleon Bonaparte, a general of the Revolution who had crowned himself emperor in 1804, controlled most of Europe.
exemplar.claim: Napoleon's empire shows the enduring issue of Imperialism, because France ruled other peoples' lands directly or through rulers it controlled.
exemplar.evidence: Document 8 shows the map's key marking the “French Empire” in dark gray and using stripes for each “Country indirectly controlled by Napoleon,” like Spain, the Confederation of the Rhine and the Grand Duchy of Warsaw.
exemplar.explain: Spain, Warsaw and the German states didn't choose French rule; Napoleon took it. Imperialism is a stronger country taking control of other lands and peoples, and this map shows most of a continent under one emperor.

u1.context: In 1812, Napoleon Bonaparte, a general of the Revolution who had crowned himself emperor in 1804, controlled most of Europe.
u1.claim: Napoleon's empire shows the enduring issue of Imperialism, because France ruled other peoples' lands directly or through rulers it controlled.
u1.evidence: Document 8 shows the map's key marking the “French Empire” in dark gray and using stripes for each “Country indirectly controlled by Napoleon,” like Spain, the Confederation of the Rhine and the Grand Duchy of Warsaw.
u1.explain: Spain, Warsaw and the German states didn't choose French rule; Napoleon took it. Imperialism is a stronger country taking control of other lands and peoples, and this map shows most of a continent under one emperor.

u2.context: In 1812, France had been at war with almost all of Europe for more than a decade, in the Napoleonic Wars. Every border on this map was drawn by war.
u2.claim: Napoleon's empire shows the enduring issue of Conflict, because it was built, and lost, through war.
u2.evidence: Document 8 shows battle sites across Europe: Austerlitz (1805) and Friedland (1807) as the empire grew, then Borodino (1812), Leipzig (1813) and Waterloo (1815).
u2.explain: The early battles built the empire and the later ones tore it down, ending at Waterloo. Conflict decided who ruled Europe, and the land France took by war it also lost by war.

links.why: The same empire reached Spain, and through Spain, a whole continent across the ocean.
links.explain: Both Napoleon's Europe and Spain's American colonies were claimed by Napoleon's family empire. However, in Europe his armies held those lands by force, while across the ocean Spanish Americans refused his brother as king and took over their own governments.

stops.title: The Haitian Revolution
stops.what_happened: Enslaved people in the French colony of Saint-Domingue rise up, and Toussaint L'Ouverture leads them in the name of Liberty and Equality. In 1804 Jean-Jacques Dessalines declares the independent nation of Haiti.

document.title: Toussaint L'Ouverture writes to the people of Saint-Domingue
document.citation: Source: C. L. R. James, Lettres de Toussaint L'Ouverture, The Black Jacobins, The Dial Press (adapted), from the New Visions Global History II Exam Question Bank, Part 1, citing the NYS Global History and Geography Regents Exam, January 2009

also_read.title: Jean-Jacques Dessalines declares Haiti independent
also_read.citation: Source: Jean-Jacques Dessalines, Haitian Declaration of Independence, January 1, 1804 (excerpt), from New Visions lesson G2.02.D.2

on_lines.reason: Dessalines calls on the people of "the country of our birth" to "live independent or die."
on_lines.question: Who a people say they are, and who that leaves out.

on_lines.reason: Dessalines names two centuries of bloodshed and swears to end any hope of re-enslaving them.
on_lines.question: Who holds authority, and what happens to the people who did not choose them.

on_lines.reason: Toussaint wants "Liberty and Equality" to reign, the French Revolution's own words, carried across the Atlantic.
on_lines.question: Who a people say they are, and who that leaves out.

on_lines.reason: Toussaint's letter is a call to arms: "Unite yourselves to us, brothers, and fight with us."
on_lines.question: Why people fight, and what is still unsettled when the fighting stops.

exemplar.context: In 1791, enslaved Africans in Saint-Domingue, France's richest colony, rose up. After years of war, they won.
exemplar.claim: The Haitian Revolution shows the enduring issue of Nationalism, because the people of Saint-Domingue fought to create their own independent nation.
exemplar.evidence: Document 2 shows Dessalines, in 1804, calling for “one last act of national authority” to secure liberty “in the country of our birth,” and declaring, “we must live independent or die.”
exemplar.explain: People who had been enslaved now call Haiti “the country of our birth” and choose independence over French rule. Nationalism is a people's push to rule itself, and Haiti became the first free Black republic.

u3-nationalism.context: In 1791, enslaved Africans in Saint-Domingue, France's richest colony, rose up. After years of war, they won.
u3-nationalism.claim: The Haitian Revolution shows the enduring issue of Nationalism, because the people of Saint-Domingue fought to create their own independent nation.
u3-nationalism.evidence: Document 2 shows Dessalines, in 1804, calling for “one last act of national authority” to secure liberty “in the country of our birth,” and declaring, “we must live independent or die.”
u3-nationalism.explain: People who had been enslaved now call Haiti “the country of our birth” and choose independence over French rule. Nationalism is a people's push to rule itself, and Haiti became the first free Black republic.

u1.context: In 1804, when Dessalines declared independence, Saint-Domingue had run on the labor of enslaved Africans for two centuries. Only two years before, France had sent an army to take back control.
u1.claim: The Haitian Revolution shows the enduring issue of Human Rights Violations, because it was a fight to end slavery for good.
u1.evidence: Document 2 shows Dessalines calling the colonizers “barbarians who have bloodied our land for two centuries,” and saying Haiti must take away “any hope of re-enslaving us.”
u1.explain: Slavery takes away every right a person should have: life, freedom and safety. Dessalines declares independence so that no government can ever take those rights away again.

u3-cultural-exchange-and-diffusion.context: In 1789, the French Revolution declared that men are born free and equal in rights. News of it crossed the Atlantic to France's colony of Saint-Domingue.
u3-cultural-exchange-and-diffusion.claim: Toussaint L'Ouverture's letter shows the enduring issue of Cultural Exchange and Diffusion, because the ideas of the French Revolution spread to the Caribbean.
u3-cultural-exchange-and-diffusion.evidence: Document 1 shows Toussaint writing, “I want Liberty and Equality to reign in San Domingo,” using the French Revolution's own words.
u3-cultural-exchange-and-diffusion.explain: Ideas don't stay where they start. Liberty and Equality traveled from Paris to the Caribbean, and enslaved people used them to fight for their own freedom.

u2.context: In 1793, Saint-Domingue was at war: enslaved people against planters, with France, Spain and Britain all fighting over the colony.
u2.claim: Toussaint's letter shows the enduring issue of Conflict, because freedom in Saint-Domingue would have to be won by fighting.
u2.evidence: Document 1 shows Toussaint writing, “I have undertaken vengeance,” and calling on others: “Unite yourselves to us, brothers, and fight with us for the same cause.”
u2.explain: Toussaint knows no one will hand over freedom, so he calls people to war. The fighting lasted until 1804, when Haiti won its independence.

links.why: Haiti wins its independence; in 1815 Bolívar plans South America's.
links.explain: The Haitian Revolution contributed to Bolívar's fight because Haiti showed that a colony in the Americas could defeat a European army and win its independence. In 1816, the year after the Jamaica Letter, Haiti gave Bolívar ships, soldiers and weapons.

stops._note: Two documents, one event. The map's widest crossing so far: four issues on three lines.

stops.title: Napoleon takes Spain, and Spanish America breaks away
stops.what_happened: Napoleon invades Spain and gives its crown to his brother Joseph. Spanish Americans refuse the French king, take over their own local governments, and their rebellion becomes a fight for independence.

document.title: A historian on what Napoleon started in Spanish America
document.citation: Source: Robert J. Alexander, Latin America, Scholastic Book Services, from the New Visions Global History II Exam Question Bank, Part 1, citing the NYS Global History and Geography Regents Exam, January 2005

on_lines.reason: "At a stroke," Spain's American colonies become part of Napoleon's family empire.
on_lines.question: Who holds authority, and what happens to the people who did not choose them.

on_lines.reason: Spanish Americans refuse a foreign king and take control of their own local governments.
on_lines.question: Who a people say they are, and who that leaves out.

exemplar.context: In 1808, Napoleon invaded Spain, which had ruled a huge empire in the Americas, from Mexico to Argentina, for three hundred years.
exemplar.claim: Napoleon's takeover of Spain shows the enduring issue of Imperialism, because millions of Spanish Americans suddenly had a foreign ruler they never chose.
exemplar.evidence: Document 3 shows that Napoleon “presented the Spanish crown to his brother Joseph,” and that “at a stroke, Spanish America became part of the Bonaparte family empire.”
exemplar.explain: One family in France now claimed a whole continent across the ocean. That is imperialism: people ruled by a stronger power far away, with no say in who it is.

u1.context: In 1808, Napoleon invaded Spain, which had ruled a huge empire in the Americas, from Mexico to Argentina, for three hundred years.
u1.claim: Napoleon's takeover of Spain shows the enduring issue of Imperialism, because millions of Spanish Americans suddenly had a foreign ruler they never chose.
u1.evidence: Document 3 shows that Napoleon “presented the Spanish crown to his brother Joseph,” and that “at a stroke, Spanish America became part of the Bonaparte family empire.”
u1.explain: One family in France now claimed a whole continent across the ocean. That is imperialism: people ruled by a stronger power far away, with no say in who it is.

u3.context: In 1808, Spanish Americans had been ruled from Spain for three hundred years. When Napoleon put his brother on Spain's throne, they had to decide where their loyalty lay.
u3.claim: The reaction in Spanish America shows the enduring issue of Nationalism, because Spanish Americans began to govern themselves.
u3.evidence: Document 3 shows that Spanish Americans “refused to accept Joseph Bonaparte as their king” and “seized control of their local governments,” and that their rebellion “turned into a revolution for complete independence.”
u3.explain: Once they ran their own governments, Spanish Americans saw they didn't need a king across the ocean. Nationalism grows when a people decide to rule themselves, and the historian says there could be “no turning back.”

links.why: Seven years later, Bolívar says independence will take union.
links.explain: Napoleon's takeover of Spain contributed to Bolívar's war because it gave Spanish Americans the chance to run their own governments. Once they had, there was no going back, and by 1815 Bolívar was leading a war for complete independence.

stops.title: Bolívar's Jamaica Letter
stops.what_happened: Simón Bolívar, in exile in Jamaica, writes that Spanish America can drive out Spain only if it unites. He pictures a free nation that will one day welcome the arts and sciences.

document.title: Simón Bolívar, the Jamaica Letter
document.citation: Source: Simón Bolívar, “Reply of a South American to a Gentleman of This Island [Jamaica],” September 6, 1815 (adapted), from the New Visions Global History II Exam Question Bank, Part 1, citing the NYS Global History and Geography II Regents Exam, August 2019

on_lines.reason: Bolívar says Spanish Americans must stand together to "found a free government" of their own.
on_lines.question: Who a people say they are, and who that leaves out.

on_lines.reason: He plans the war to "expel the Spaniards," against an enemy with far more military supplies.
on_lines.question: Why people fight, and what is still unsettled when the fighting stops.

exemplar.context: In 1815, Spain had crushed the first independence movements in South America, and Simón Bolívar was living in exile in Jamaica. He wrote a letter explaining what South America would need to win.
exemplar.claim: Bolívar's Jamaica Letter shows the enduring issue of Nationalism, because he says Spanish Americans must unite to build their own nation.
exemplar.evidence: Document 4 shows Bolívar writing that to “expel the Spaniards and to found a free government,” what they need is “union, obviously.”
exemplar.explain: Bolívar knows separate colonies can't beat Spain alone, so he asks them to see themselves as one people. Nationalism is that loyalty to a nation of your own, and Bolívar wants it to become a free government.

u3.context: In 1815, Spain had crushed the first independence movements in South America, and Simón Bolívar was living in exile in Jamaica. He wrote a letter explaining what South America would need to win.
u3.claim: Bolívar's Jamaica Letter shows the enduring issue of Nationalism, because he says Spanish Americans must unite to build their own nation.
u3.evidence: Document 4 shows Bolívar writing that to “expel the Spaniards and to found a free government,” what they need is “union, obviously.”
u3.explain: Bolívar knows separate colonies can't beat Spain alone, so he asks them to see themselves as one people. Nationalism is that loyalty to a nation of your own, and Bolívar wants it to become a free government.

u2.context: In 1815, the wars for independence in South America were going badly, and Bolívar was in exile in Jamaica.
u2.claim: Bolívar's Jamaica Letter shows the enduring issue of Conflict, because independence would have to be won in a war against a stronger enemy.
u2.evidence: Document 4 shows Bolívar warning that America “is attacked by Spain, which has more military supplies than any we can possibly acquire.”
u2.explain: Spanish America has no allies and fewer weapons, so the fight will be long and hard. Conflict is how this independence gets decided, and Bolívar went on to lead the armies that won it.

links.why: In Italy, Cavour also says a divided people must unite before it can be free and strong.
links.explain: Both Bolívar and Cavour said a divided people had to unite before it could be free and strong. However, Bolívar called on Spanish Americans to unite against Spain, an empire across the ocean, while Cavour called on Italians to unite the small states of their own peninsula.

stops.title: Cavour: one Italy
stops.what_happened: Camillo di Cavour, who later led the unification of Italy, writes that Italians must silence the small questions that divide them. A united Italy, he argues, could stand with the most civilized nations.

document.title: Camillo di Cavour, 1846
document.citation: Source: Camillo di Cavour, 1846, from the New Visions Global History II Exam Question Bank, Part 1, citing the NYS Global History and Geography Regents Exam, August 2003

on_lines.reason: Cavour wants Italians to set aside what divides them and build one nation, "glorious and powerful."
on_lines.question: Who a people say they are, and who that leaves out.

exemplar.context: In 1846, Italy was split into many small states, with Austria ruling the north and the pope ruling the middle. Cavour, from the Kingdom of Sardinia, wanted one Italy.
exemplar.claim: Cavour's writing shows the enduring issue of Nationalism, because he calls on Italians to set aside what divides them and build one nation.
exemplar.evidence: Document 5 shows Cavour writing that in the face of “this great question,” Italian unity, “all the petty questions that divide us must be silenced,” so that Italy can be “glorious and powerful.”
exemplar.explain: Cavour wants Italians to think of themselves as one people first. That loyalty to a shared nation is nationalism, and by 1870 it had united Italy.

links.why: Germany unites too, but Bismarck says it will take blood and iron.
links.explain: Both Cavour and Bismarck led a powerful kingdom, Sardinia and Prussia, in uniting many small states into one nation. However, Cavour asked Italians to silence the petty questions that divide them, while Bismarck said Germany would be united by blood and iron.

stops.title: Bismarck: blood and iron
stops.what_happened: Otto von Bismarck, leading Prussia, says Germany will be united by blood and iron, not by democracy. Three wars later, in 1871, it is.

document.title: Otto von Bismarck, 1862
document.citation: Source: Otto von Bismarck, speech to the Prussian parliament, 1862 (adapted), from the New Visions Global History II Exam Question Bank, Part 1, citing the NYS Global History and Geography Regents Exam

on_lines.reason: Bismarck's goal is one German nation, and he says exactly how he will get it.
on_lines.question: Who a people say they are, and who that leaves out.

on_lines.reason: "Blood and iron" means war; he puts force ahead of "democracy or liberal standards."
on_lines.question: Why people fight, and what is still unsettled when the fighting stops.

exemplar.context: In 1862, Germany was still split into dozens of states, and Prussia and Austria were the strongest. Otto von Bismarck had just become Prussia's leader.
exemplar.claim: Bismarck's speech shows the enduring issue of Nationalism, because his goal was one German nation, led by Prussia.
exemplar.evidence: Document 6 shows Bismarck telling the Prussian parliament, “Not by democracy or liberal standards will our goal be achieved but by blood and iron.”
exemplar.explain: His “goal” is a united Germany, and he will do whatever it takes to reach it. By 1871 the German states were one nation under Prussia's king.

u3.context: In 1862, Germany was still split into dozens of states, and Prussia and Austria were the strongest. Otto von Bismarck had just become Prussia's leader.
u3.claim: Bismarck's speech shows the enduring issue of Nationalism, because his goal was one German nation, led by Prussia.
u3.evidence: Document 6 shows Bismarck telling the Prussian parliament, “Not by democracy or liberal standards will our goal be achieved but by blood and iron.”
u3.explain: His “goal” is a united Germany, and he will do whatever it takes to reach it. By 1871 the German states were one nation under Prussia's king.

u2.context: In 1862, Prussia wanted to unite the German states, but Austria and France stood in the way. Bismarck believed only war could settle it.
u2.claim: Bismarck's speech shows the enduring issue of Conflict, because he planned to unite Germany by war.
u2.evidence: Document 6 shows Bismarck saying the goal will be won “not by democracy or liberal standards” but “by blood and iron.”
u2.explain: Blood and iron means soldiers and weapons. Bismarck fought three wars, against Denmark, Austria and France, and Germany was united in 1871 because Prussia won them.

links.why: The same force that unites Germany is pulling Austria-Hungary apart.
links.explain: Both German unification and the Balkan crisis were driven by nationalism. However, in Germany nationalism joined many states into one nation, while in Austria-Hungary and the Balkans it was pulling an empire apart.

stops.title: The Balkans reach the boiling point
stops.what_happened: Austria-Hungary rules many peoples inside one border, and small Balkan nations are pushing to drive out the Ottoman Empire. In 1912 a British cartoon shows Europe's great powers trying to sit on the lid of a boiling pot.

document.title: “The Boiling Point,” Punch, October 2, 1912
document.citation: Source: Leonard Raven-Hill, “The Boiling Point,” Punch (London), October 2, 1912 (public domain)

also_read.title: Map: the peoples of Austria-Hungary, 1911
also_read.citation: Source: William R. Shepherd, “Distribution of Races in Austria-Hungary,” Historical Atlas, Henry Holt, 1911 (public domain)

on_lines.reason: The map shows many peoples inside one empire's border, each with its own claim to be a nation.
on_lines.question: Who a people say they are, and who that leaves out.

on_lines.reason: The cartoon's pot of "Balkan Troubles" is about to boil over, and the great powers can't hold the lid down.
on_lines.question: Why people fight, and what is still unsettled when the fighting stops.

exemplar.context: In 1911, Austria-Hungary ruled many different peoples inside one border, and the Balkan peoples were pushing the Ottoman Empire out. Each group wanted a nation of its own.
exemplar.claim: The map of Austria-Hungary shows the enduring issue of Nationalism, because many peoples lived inside one empire, and each could claim to be a nation.
exemplar.evidence: Document 7 shows a legend listing ten peoples, including Germans, Magyars, Czechs, Poles and Rumanians, with six of them grouped under the word Slavs.
exemplar.explain: Each of those peoples had its own language and could demand its own state. Nationalism pulled Germany and Italy together, but here it was pulling an empire apart.

u3.context: In 1911, Austria-Hungary ruled many different peoples inside one border, and the Balkan peoples were pushing the Ottoman Empire out. Each group wanted a nation of its own.
u3.claim: The map of Austria-Hungary shows the enduring issue of Nationalism, because many peoples lived inside one empire, and each could claim to be a nation.
u3.evidence: Document 7 shows a legend listing ten peoples, including Germans, Magyars, Czechs, Poles and Rumanians, with six of them grouped under the word Slavs.
u3.explain: Each of those peoples had its own language and could demand its own state. Nationalism pulled Germany and Italy together, but here it was pulling an empire apart.

u2.context: In 1912, the Balkan states were about to go to war with the Ottoman Empire, and Europe's great powers had interests on every side. Days after this cartoon ran, the First Balkan War began.
u2.claim: “The Boiling Point” shows the enduring issue of Conflict, because the Balkans were about to explode into war.
u2.evidence: Document 8 shows a pot labeled “BALKAN TROUBLES” with steam pouring out, and five men pressing on the lid to keep it closed.
u2.explain: The great powers can't hold the lid on much longer, and the steam is already escaping. The fighting that started in the Balkans would lead to World War I two years later.

stops._note: Documents 7 and 8 are one event; the cartoon leads. The First Balkan War began days after the cartoon ran.
